items.prompt: What actually stops a tree from growing much taller than the tallest coast redwoods, which top 115 metres?

options.label: There isn't enough sunlight higher up to make the extra height worthwhile
options.feedback: Sunlight is, if anything, more abundant above the canopy than below it, so a shortage of light isn't what caps a tree's height.

options.label: A physical limit on how high water can be pulled up through narrow tubes without the column of water snapping apart
options.feedback: Water rising through a trunk is held together by its own molecules, and past a certain height the pull needed to keep lifting it comes close to tearing that column apart.

options.label: The roots run out of minerals to absorb once a tree passes a certain height
options.feedback: Minerals needed in a leaf are a tiny quantity compared with water, and mineral supply isn't what tracks so closely with a tree's maximum height.

options.label: The trunk becomes too heavy for the roots to anchor
options.feedback: Root anchoring failure shows up as a tree toppling in wind, not as a ceiling on how tall a healthy, upright tree can grow in calm conditions.

items.ok_title: A limit written into the plumbing
items.ok_line: Height runs into the physics of how high a water column can be pulled without breaking.
items.ko_line: The ceiling on tree height comes from how water is transported upward, not from what's available at the top or the load at the base.
items.exp_text: A tree lifts water upward by evaporation at the leaves pulling on a continuous, unbroken thread of water inside its narrow transport tubes, held together by the way water molecules cling to each other. The higher that column has to be pulled, the greater the strain on it, and past a certain height the pulling force needed comes close to the point where the column would tear apart inside the tube. Coast redwoods growing near that ceiling show just how close a living plumbing system can get to its own breaking point before the whole method stops working.

items.prompt: The giant sequoia known as General Sherman is the most massive single-trunk tree on Earth by wood volume. What lets a giant sequoia keep adding that much wood for thousands of years instead of dying young like most trees?

options.label: It grows in soil richer in nutrients than any other forest on Earth
options.feedback: Giant sequoias grow in fairly ordinary mountain soil; the advantage isn't an unusually rich nutrient supply but survival of the trunk itself over an extremely long time.

options.label: It photosynthesises at a faster rate than any other tree species
options.feedback: A giant sequoia's rate of making sugar per leaf isn't exceptional among trees; what's exceptional is how many centuries it keeps a working trunk to spend that sugar building.

options.label: Its bark is unusually thick and fire-resistant, and its wood resists rot, so damage that would kill other trees rarely reaches its living tissue
options.feedback: A trunk protected from both fire and decay for centuries keeps its thin working layer of living tissue intact, letting the tree simply carry on adding wood year after year.

options.label: Its wood is far denser than that of other conifers, so it reaches record volume with less actual growth
options.feedback: Sequoia wood is in fact fairly light and soft for a conifer; volume records come from sheer accumulated size over time, not from unusually dense wood.

items.ok_title: Protected long enough to keep piling on wood
items.ok_line: Surviving fire and decay for centuries is what lets the growth simply continue.
items.ko_title: Not richer soil, faster growth, or denser wood
items.ko_line: The advantage is about staying alive and undamaged for an extraordinarily long stretch, not about any one growth process running faster.
items.exp_title: Outliving the usual causes of death
items.exp_text: A tree's thin, living cambium layer keeps adding wood every year for as long as it survives, so total size mostly comes down to how long that layer stays alive and undamaged. A giant sequoia's bark can grow extremely thick and is soaked with compounds that resist both fire and fungal decay, so injuries that would let disease into another species's trunk usually can't reach a sequoia's living tissue. With fire and decay largely held off from ever reaching its cambium, the tree simply keeps doing what every tree does every year, for as long as that thin living layer stays intact.

items.prompt: Bristlecone pines in the mountains of the western United States include the oldest known living trees, some over 4,800 years old. Why doesn't a tree wear out with age the way an animal's body does?

options.label: A tree's cells never divide after it first sprouts, so there's nothing left to wear out
options.feedback: The opposite is true: a tree's growing tissue keeps dividing and producing brand-new cells throughout its entire life, which is part of why it doesn't wear out the way a body of cells that stopped renewing would.

options.label: Its wood is chemically immune to any kind of decay or damage
options.feedback: Even a bristlecone pine's wood can rot or burn under the wrong conditions; immunity to all damage isn't the reason for its age, since plenty of individual bristlecone pines do die.

options.label: It grows so slowly that its cells barely change from year to year
options.feedback: Slow growth doesn't stop cells from changing; what matters is that the tree's living tissue is freshly remade each year rather than the same aging cells persisting for centuries.

options.label: Only the tree's thin layer of actively growing tissue needs to stay alive, and each year it produces entirely fresh cells rather than the old ones simply persisting
options.feedback: The bulk of an ancient trunk is dead structural wood, while the living, working part is a thin renewing layer making brand-new cells every year, so the tree's functioning tissue is never actually old.

items.ok_line: The living part of the tree is remade fresh every single year.
items.ko_title: Not frozen cells, not immunity, not slowness
items.ko_line: Ask which part of the tree is actually alive at any moment, and how old that particular part really is.
items.exp_title: Only the newest layer has to survive
items.exp_text: Almost all of an ancient trunk is dead wood, holding the tree upright but doing no living work at all, while the tree's actual living tissue is confined to a thin layer just under the bark. That layer doesn't sit there ageing for millennia — it divides every year, producing brand-new cells that take over the job of growth and transport while the previous year's cells harden into more dead wood. As long as that one thin ring of freshly made tissue survives each season's threats, the tree as a whole can keep going indefinitely, however old the dead wood stacked up inside it becomes.

items.prompt: The Árbol del Tule in Mexico has one of the widest tree trunks ever measured, with a girth over 36 metres. Some botanists think part of that width comes from the trunk actually being several trees fused together. How could separate trees end up fused into what looks like a single trunk?

options.label: Neighbouring trunks growing side by side kept thickening year after year until their expanding wood pressed together and grew into one continuous mass
options.feedback: Each trunk's cambium kept adding wood outward exactly as it would alone, and where two expanding trunks met and pressed against each other for long enough, their tissues grew into and around one another as if joining into a single trunk.

options.label: Seeds from several trees landed in the exact same spot and grew intertwined from the very start
options.feedback: Seeds landing close together would produce separate seedlings competing side by side, not the smoothly continuous trunk surface a fused tree shows once it has thickened for centuries.

options.label: Lightning strikes fused their trunks together instantly
options.feedback: A lightning strike scars or splits wood rather than welding two separate trunks into one continuous mass; that kind of joining takes place gradually as living tissue keeps expanding against itself, not in an instant.

options.label: One tree's roots grew up and around the other tree's trunk from below
options.feedback: This kind of fusion is described happening above ground between adjacent trunks growing outward into each other, not as one tree's roots wrapping around another's trunk from underneath.

items.ok_title: Two trunks growing into each other
items.ok_line: Ordinary yearly thickening, on two neighbours close enough to meet, is enough to join them.
items.ko_title: Not instant, not seeds, not roots
items.ko_line: This is the same yearly-thickening mechanism as any trunk getting wider, just applied to two trunks growing close enough to run into one another.
items.exp_title: Thickening until there's no gap left
items.exp_text: Every trunk widens a little every year as its cambium adds a fresh layer of wood just under the bark, pushing the surface slightly further outward each time. If two separate trees happen to be growing close enough together, that steady outward thickening eventually brings their surfaces into contact, and continued growth presses the two trunks against each other rather than letting either expand freely outward. Kept up over centuries, that pressure and continued layering can knit the touching wood and bark of both trunks together until the boundary between them all but disappears from the outside.

items.prompt: Some tree species, such as certain fast-growing paulownias, can add several metres of new height in a single year, far outpacing most other trees. What allows a species like this to shoot upward so quickly?

options.label: It photosynthesises through its bark as well as its leaves, doubling its sugar supply
options.feedback: Bark is not built for capturing light the way leaf tissue is, and a fast-growing species doesn't gain some extra sugar-making surface this way; its speed comes from how it spends the sugar it makes, not from making more of it through the bark.

options.label: It skips the stage of building a growing tip and instead extends along its whole length at once
options.feedback: Every shoot, fast-growing or not, still lengthens from a growing tip at its end; a fast species doesn't abandon that point of growth, it simply produces new cells there unusually quickly.

options.label: It builds unusually large, hollow, lightweight cells very quickly, trading strength for speed of extension
options.feedback: Cells this large and light take relatively little material to build compared with the sturdy, dense cells most trees invest in, so the same amount of sugar stretches a shoot much further, much faster.

options.label: Its roots draw water under much higher pressure than other trees, forcing the shoot to stretch
options.feedback: Root water pressure isn't what stretches a shoot upward; the shoot lengthens by cell growth at its tip, and root pressure playing a driving role in that speed isn't the mechanism here.

items.ok_line: Trading sturdiness for speed lets a shoot stretch a long way on a limited sugar budget.
items.ko_title: Not extra light-catching, no shortcut tip, not root pressure
items.ko_line: The speed comes from how efficiently the growing tip's new cells are built, not from an extra source of sugar or an unusual driving pressure.
items.exp_text: A shoot's growing tip still has to build every new cell from the sugar the tree has on hand, and a small, dense, thick-walled cell costs far more material and time to build than a large, thin-walled, mostly hollow one. A fast-growing species builds the second kind, so the same daily sugar budget stretches the shoot much further because each cell demands so little material relative to the length it adds. The result is height added at a pace few other trees can match, at the cost of wood that stays notably weaker until it thickens and matures years later.

items.prompt: The boreal forest, or taiga, stretching across Russia, Canada and Scandinavia, is the largest connected forest biome on Earth. What single climate pattern shapes almost everything about the trees able to survive across that entire band?

options.label: Extremely heavy year-round rainfall
options.feedback: Much of this region actually receives fairly modest precipitation; heavy year-round rainfall isn't the defining pressure shaping which trees survive there.

options.label: A short growing season bracketed by long, severely cold winters
options.feedback: Only trees able to complete their yearly growth in a brief warm stretch, and then endure months of hard freezing cold, can persist right across this band, and that single pattern shapes which species dominate it.

options.label: Frequent flooding from major rivers
options.feedback: Flooding affects certain river valleys locally, but it isn't the pattern spanning the entire band of forest across three continents; something far more universal across that whole area is doing the shaping.

options.label: Constant volcanic ash improving the soil
options.feedback: Volcanic activity isn't a consistent feature across this vast band of forest at all; whatever shapes tree survival here has to apply uniformly across the whole region, not just near occasional volcanoes.

items.ok_title: A brief summer, a brutal winter
items.ok_line: Only trees built to survive that exact rhythm dominate across the whole band.
items.ko_title: Not rainfall, flooding, or volcanic soil
items.ko_line: The one pattern that applies uniformly across this entire stretch of the globe is the length and severity of its seasons.
items.exp_title: One climate rhythm, repeated across three continents
items.exp_text: This band of forest circles the globe at a latitude where summers are short and winters are long, dark and severely cold, a pattern that holds fairly consistently whether you're in Siberia, Canada or northern Scandinavia. Trees able to dominate here need to complete a year's worth of growth in a brief warm window and then survive months of hard freezing afterward, which strongly favours a narrow set of cold-tolerant conifers over almost anything else. That single, repeating seasonal rhythm, more than soil, rainfall or any local feature, is what ties this enormous stretch of forest into one recognisable biome.

items.prompt: A wild fig tree at Echo Caves in South Africa has been recorded with roots reaching more than 120 metres below the surface, among the deepest ever traced for any tree. What drove its roots to grow that deep?

options.label: The tree needed the extra depth purely for anchoring against strong winds
options.feedback: A wide-spreading network of shallower roots anchors a tree against wind more effectively than one narrow root pushing straight down; anchoring isn't what would drive a root this deep.

options.label: Underground caves pulled the roots downward with lower air pressure
options.feedback: Roots don't respond to air pressure differences underground; a root's growth is steered by things like moisture and oxygen levels in the soil around it, not by pressure gradients.

options.label: The tree was planted in a hole that deep to begin with
options.feedback: A tree's roots grow outward and downward from a seedling's original position over the course of its life; the depth reached here reflects decades of ongoing root growth, not the depth of an original planting hole.

options.label: The roots followed cracks in the underlying rock in a continuing search for water, since the surrounding surface soil offered too little
options.feedback: A root tip keeps steering toward wherever moisture is available, and where the surface and shallow soil are too dry, that steering can carry roots down through cracks in rock for an extraordinary distance.

items.ok_title: Chasing water through cracks in the rock
items.ok_line: A root keeps steering toward moisture, however far down that moisture happens to be.
items.ko_title: Not wind anchoring, not pressure, not planting depth
items.ko_line: The driving factor here is the same one steering any root tip day to day: where the moisture actually is.
items.exp_title: Following moisture as far as it goes
items.exp_text: A root tip constantly steers toward whichever side of it has more available moisture, growing faster where conditions are drier and slower where they're wetter, which curves its path toward water over time. In dry, thin surface soil sitting above fractured limestone, the nearest reliable moisture can lie deep down inside cracks in the rock itself, so a root chasing that signal keeps extending downward through the cracks it finds. Given enough time, and cracks leading far enough down, that same everyday steering mechanism can carry a root system to remarkable depth.

items.prompt: The raffia palm produces fronds up to 25 metres long, the longest leaves of any plant. How does a single leaf reach that length without collapsing under its own weight?

options.label: It isn't one flat blade at all, but a long central rib lined with many smaller leaflets, so its strength comes from a rigid spine rather than a single wide surface
options.feedback: A thick central rib running the whole length acts like a beam, holding up rows of much smaller, lighter leaflets branching off it, rather than one enormous fragile sheet trying to support itself.

options.label: It is kept rigid by being packed full of water under high pressure
options.feedback: Water pressure inside plant cells does give ordinary leaves some of their firmness, but a leaf of this length relies on an actual rigid supporting structure, not simply higher internal water pressure, to keep from collapsing.

options.label: It grows resting flat along the ground so weight is never an issue
options.feedback: These fronds extend outward and upward from the crown of the palm rather than trailing along the ground, so weight and support genuinely are a real structural problem this leaf has to solve while standing up from the trunk.

options.label: Its surface is thin enough that the whole leaf weighs almost nothing
options.feedback: A leaf spanning this much length, even with thin tissue, still adds up to considerable weight; the way that weight is held up and distributed along a central rib, not simple thinness, is what keeps it from failing.

items.ok_line: A rigid central rib carries the load, with many small leaflets attached along it.
items.ko_title: Not water pressure, ground support, or sheer thinness
items.ko_line: Think about what an enormously long leaf would need structurally that a single flat blade of the same length couldn't provide on its own.
items.exp_text: Rather than growing as one continuous flat blade, this kind of frond is built around a long, thick, rigid central rib running its whole length, acting much like the spine of a structure carrying a load. Many separate, individually small and light leaflets branch off that rib along its sides, so the leaf's total light-catching surface is distributed across many manageable pieces instead of concentrated in one unsupported sheet. That division of a huge total leaf into a strong central support plus many small attachments is what lets the whole structure reach such extraordinary length while still holding itself up from the crown of the palm.

items.prompt: In Utah, a single quaking aspen colony known as Pando covers more than 40 hectares with tens of thousands of individual-looking trunks, yet is counted as one single organism. How can what looks like an entire forest actually be one organism?

options.label: Every trunk grew from the same seed, scattered across the whole area at once
options.feedback: A scattering of seeds from one parent would still produce many genetically distinct seedlings, each its own separate organism, rather than one single connected individual.

options.label: The trunks are physically fused together above ground into one connected trunk
options.feedback: These trunks stand apart from each other above ground, each looking like its own separate tree; the connection that makes them one organism runs underground through the shared roots, not through any above-ground fusion.

options.label: Every trunk sprouted upward from one continuous, shared root system, making them genetically identical extensions of the same plant rather than separate trees
options.feedback: Each trunk is a new shoot rising from the same spreading underground root system, sharing identical genetic material with every other trunk rather than being a separate tree grown from its own seed.

options.label: A fungus links the trunks together and controls them as one unit
options.feedback: A shared fungal network can link separate trees' roots for exchanging resources, but that's not what makes this particular colony count as a single organism; here, the trunks are all genetically identical shoots from one shared root system, not separate individuals joined by a fungus.

items.ok_line: Every trunk is a shoot off the same shared roots, genetically identical to all the rest.
items.ko_title: Not a scattering of seeds, not fused trunks, not a fungal link
items.ko_line: The connection making this one organism runs underground, through a shared and spreading root system common to every trunk.
items.exp_title: Thousands of shoots, one root system
items.exp_text: Instead of growing from separate seeds, this colony spreads by sending up new trunks directly from an ever-extending shared root system, so each new trunk is genetically identical to every other one already standing. What looks from above like a dense forest of individual trees is really just the visible, above-ground portion of one continuously connected plant, repeated tens of thousands of times over. As long as that shared root system stays alive underground, it can keep sending up fresh trunks to replace any that die, letting the organism as a whole keep spreading long after any one trunk above it has come and gone.

items.prompt: Black ironwood is among the densest woods known, dense enough to sink rather than float in water. What actually makes one wood sink while most other woods float?

options.label: It absorbs so much water while the tree is alive that it never dries out, even after being cut
options.feedback: Freshly cut wood from any species holds a good deal of water at first, but wood is generally left to dry before being measured for how it compares to water; what makes this wood exceptional is the solid structure of the wood itself, not water it happens to be carrying.

options.label: It contains traces of minerals absorbed from unusually mineral-rich soil
options.feedback: A trace amount of absorbed minerals wouldn't come close to shifting a whole log's density enough to make it sink; the difference lies in how the wood's own cells are built, not in what minerals happen to be mixed into it.

options.label: Its bark is thick enough to trap air pockets that later fill with water
options.feedback: Whether a whole log sinks or floats is decided by the density of the wood itself, and bark trapping air pockets that later fill with water isn't the mechanism responsible for a wood this dense sinking.

options.label: Its wood cells have unusually thick walls and very little open, air-filled space inside them, packing far more solid material into the same volume than most wood does
options.feedback: Most wood floats because its cells enclose a lot of empty, air-filled space inside thin walls; where the walls are unusually thick and that internal space is minimal, a given volume of wood packs in enough solid material to weigh more than the same volume of water.

items.ok_title: Almost no empty space left inside
items.ok_line: Thick cell walls and little trapped air pack in more solid material per given volume.
items.ko_line: Whether a piece of wood sinks or floats comes down to how much solid material versus empty space its own cells actually contain.
items.exp_title: Barely any air left to make it float
items.exp_text: Ordinary wood floats because its cells are built with fairly thin walls surrounding a good deal of empty, air-filled internal space, which keeps the overall material lighter than an equal volume of water. This wood's cells instead have unusually thick walls and very little of that hollow interior space, so a given volume of it packs in far more actual solid plant material than most wood does. With so little empty space left to lighten it, a piece of this wood ends up denser than water itself, which is why it sinks instead of floating.
